etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “whiteness” or “pavement”, likely from the white poplar or from white chalk soil.
biblical_def: Libnah was a royal Canaanite city of the Shephelah, the lowland country of Judah, smitten by Joshua in the great southern campaign. After taking Makkedah, Joshua turned upon Libnah, and the LORD “delivered it also, and the king thereof, into the hand of Israel” (Jos 10:30). The conquest of Libnah belongs to that sweep of victories in which God fought for His people, fulfilling His covenant promise of the land. In the allotment Libnah fell within Judah’s portion (Jos 15:42), and it was afterward set apart as one of the cities of the priests, the sons of Aaron, a Levitical city given out of the tribe of Judah (Jos 21:13). Thus a stronghold once devoted to idolatry became a dwelling of those who ministered before the altar — a fit picture of grace turning rebel ground into holy ground. In the days of Joram king of Judah, when that king had forsaken the LORD, “Libnah revolted at the same time” (2Ki 8:22), a chastening sign that disobedience in the throne loosens the kingdom at its borders. Libnah is later named in Sennacherib’s march against Hezekiah (2Ki 19:8). The town stands as a witness that the land was not won by Israel’s sword but given by Israel’s God, and that priestly cities were planted as lamps of worship throughout the inheritance.
webster_summary: A royal Canaanite city of the Judahite lowland, taken by Joshua and afterward made a Levitical city of the priests.

corruption_summary: The lesson worth recovering is that the land was God’s gift, and that disobedience at the throne unsettles the kingdom to its borders.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Libnah is twofold: first, that Israel did not seize Canaan by native strength but received it as the LORD delivered city after city into her hand; second, that a city once given to idols was sanctified into a dwelling of the priests, a standing emblem of redeeming grace.

The revolt of Libnah under King Joram preaches the same covenant truth from the dark side. When a king forsakes the God of his fathers, the realm frays at its edges; rebellion in the high place breeds rebellion in the low. The faithfulness of God is the only sure mortar of any kingdom, and the throne that abandons Him need not wonder why the borders break away.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “calf-like” or “round”, from a root related to egel, a calf.
biblical_def: Eglon was a royal Canaanite city of the southern lowland of Judah, whose king joined the confederacy that warred against Gibeon for making peace with Israel. When the Gibeonites cried to Joshua, the king of Eglon stood among the five Amorite kings — with Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, and Lachish — whom the LORD smote with a great slaughter and upon whom He cast down great hailstones from heaven (Jos 10:3, 11). After the five kings were taken in the cave at Makkedah and slain, Joshua passed from Lachish to Eglon, and “they took it on that day, and smote it with the edge of the sword” (Jos 10:34–35). The destruction was complete, utterly devoting the city as the LORD had commanded. Eglon afterward fell within the inheritance of Judah in the Shephelah (Jos 15:39). This is the city Eglon, not to be confounded with Eglon the fat king of Moab whom Ehud slew in the days of the Judges. The fall of Eglon belongs to that day of days when the sun stood still over Gibeon and the moon stayed in the valley of Ajalon, while the God of Israel fought for His people. It stands as proof that no walled city and no league of kings can stand when the LORD has decreed their overthrow and given the land to His chosen.
webster_summary: A royal Canaanite city of the Amorite coalition against Gibeon, taken and destroyed by Joshua in the southern campaign.
webster_full: EGLON, a royal city of the Amorites in the lowland of Judah, distinct from the Moabite king of the same name.
Its king joined the five-king coalition against Gibeon (Jos 10:3).

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Eglon is the certainty of God’s judgment upon a land filled with idolatry. The Canaanites were not driven out for Israel’s righteousness but because their iniquity was full; Eglon’s overthrow was the LORD’s long-patient justice come at last.

Modern readers must not be ashamed of the conquest. The same God who cast down hailstones on the Amorite kings is the righteous Judge of all the earth. The fall of Eglon warns every confederacy of men against the living God, and it comforts His people: when the LORD fights for them, the strongest walls and the proudest kings cannot stand.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “sanctuary” or “oracle”, the same word used of the innermost chamber of the temple.
biblical_def: Debir was a city of the hill country of Judah, formerly called Kirjath-sepher, the “city of the book”, and also Kirjath-sannah. Joshua smote it in the southern campaign, taking the city, its king, and all the towns about it, and utterly destroying every soul (Jos 10:38–39). Yet Debir was again held by the Anakim and had to be retaken, and Caleb offered his daughter Achsah in marriage to the man who would smite Kirjath-sepher. “And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife” (Jos 15:17; Jdg 1:13). This Othniel became the first of Israel’s judges, a deliverer raised up by the Spirit of the LORD. Achsah, the godly bride won at Debir, asked her father for springs of water to bless her dry southern inheritance, and he granted her the upper and the nether springs. Debir was afterward set apart as a Levitical city, given to the sons of Aaron (Jos 21:15). Thus the “city of the book” passed from heathen hands to become a dwelling of the priests, a fitting providence that the place once named for writing should house the keepers of the holy oracles. Debir stands as a memorial of valor rewarded, of a daughter’s wise petition, and of a city turned over to the worship of the true God.
webster_summary: A city of the Judahite hill country, also called Kirjath-sepher, taken by Othniel and made a Levitical city.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Debir is the honor God puts upon faithful courage. Othniel ventured for Caleb’s promise and won both a city and a bride; he was then raised up by the Spirit as Israel’s first judge. Faithfulness in the lesser trust prepared him for the greater.

There is sweetness too in Achsah’s wisdom. Receiving a parched inheritance, she did not murmur but asked her father for springs, and he gave her the upper and the nether springs. The believer likewise comes to the Father for the living water without which the inheritance lies dry, and the Father gives liberally to them that ask.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “house of the hollow” or “place of the cavern”, marking the steep mountain pass.
biblical_def: Beth-horon was a pair of towns, the upper and the nether, guarding the great pass that descended from the hill country of Ephraim toward the coastal plain. It was on this pass that the LORD wrought His mighty deliverance in the day Joshua fought for Gibeon. When the five Amorite kings fled before Israel, the LORD “cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword” (Jos 10:11). The descent of Beth-horon thus became a monument of God’s direct intervention in battle, the heavens themselves warring against His enemies while the sun stood still over Gibeon. The two towns lay on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin (Jos 16:3, 5) and were assigned afterward to the Kohathite Levites (Jos 21:22). For the strategic worth of the pass, Solomon fortified both, “Beth-horon the nether, and Baalath” (1Ki 9:17; 2Ch 8:5), making them strongholds of the kingdom. Through the centuries this pass remained a famous gate of war, the road by which armies climbed to or fled from Jerusalem. Beth-horon stands first and chiefly, however, as the place where God reminded Israel forever that the battle is the LORD’s, and that He hurls the very stones of heaven to scatter the foes of His covenant people.
webster_summary: A pair of towns, upper and nether, on the mountain pass where the LORD cast down great stones on the fleeing Amorites; later fortified by Solomon.

corruption_summary: The truth to recover is that the battle is the LORD’s, and that He Himself overthrows His enemies with the weapons of heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Beth-horon is plain and bracing: the LORD fights for His people. More Amorites perished by the hailstones God hurled than by the swords of Israel, that no man might boast. The victory at the pass was not Israel’s prowess but God’s power.

The same God who commanded the stones of heaven commands all His providence still. The believer who feels outnumbered upon the steep and slippery road may take heart: the heavens are not neutral. He who ordained the going down of Beth-horon orders every battle of His church, and He will not lose one of His own to the fleeing kings of darkness.

etymology: From the Hebrew gibeah, meaning “hill”; called “of Saul” because it was the home and capital of Israel’s first king.
biblical_def: Gibeah of Saul, also called Gibeah of Benjamin, was a town in the territory of Benjamin that became famous twice over — once for shame and once for honor. In the dark days of the Judges, when there was no king in Israel and every man did that which was right in his own eyes, the men of Gibeah committed the abominable outrage against the Levite’s concubine, a wickedness so vile that it provoked civil war and nearly blotted out the whole tribe of Benjamin (Jdg 19–20). The horror of Gibeah became a byword for depravity, recalled long after by the prophets (Hos 9:9; Hos 10:9). Yet from this same Benjamite town came Saul the son of Kish, whom God gave as Israel’s first king. After his anointing, “Saul also went home to Gibeah; and there went with him a band of men, whose hearts God had touched” (1Sa 10:26). Gibeah became his royal seat, the place to which the tidings of Jabesh-gilead came (1Sa 11:4), and the hill where he held his court under the tree (1Sa 22:6). The town thus stands as a double witness: of the depths to which men sink when each is his own law, and of the LORD’s patient ordering of His people’s history, raising a king even from a tribe that had once nearly destroyed itself by its own sin.
webster_summary: A town of Benjamin, home and capital of King Saul, also the scene of the Levite’s concubine outrage in the days of the Judges.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Gibeah is the bitter fruit of moral autonomy. “Every man did that which was right in his own eyes,” and Gibeah is the result — an outrage so foul it tore the nation apart. The age that despises objective law and exalts the self as the only standard is an age that breeds new Gibeahs.

Yet the same town gives a second word. From sin-stained Benjamin God raised Saul to be king, showing that He works His purposes even through unworthy material. The believer learns to dread the depravity of the human heart left to itself, and to marvel at the patient providence of God, who governs the unfolding of redemption through flawed men and shameful places.

etymology: From the Hebrew, likely meaning “place of hornets” or “wasp town”, from a root for stinging insects.
biblical_def: Zorah was a town in the lowland of Judah, on the border of the tribe of Dan, set among the hills overlooking the valley of Sorek. It is remembered above all as the home of Manoah the Danite and the birthplace of Samson, the mightiest of the judges. To Manoah’s barren wife the angel of the LORD appeared, promising a son who should be a Nazarite unto God from the womb and who should begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines (Jdg 13:2–5). The child was born and grew, “and the LORD blessed him. And the Spirit of the LORD began to move him at times in the camp of Dan between Zorah and Eshtaol” (Jdg 13:24–25). Thus Zorah marked both the cradle and the calling of Samson. There too, after his long course of strength and folly and final faithful death, his kinsmen brought his body home: “and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the buryingplace of Manoah his father” (Jdg 16:31). Zorah was listed among the cities of Judah (Jos 15:33) and afterward of Dan (Jos 19:41), and it was later fortified by Rehoboam (2Ch 11:10). The town stands as a quiet witness to the sovereign grace of God, who chooses an obscure hill village to bring forth a deliverer, and who moves His Spirit where and when He will.

corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is the sovereign grace of God, who raises a deliverer from an obscure village and moves His Spirit as He pleases.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Zorah is the freedom of God’s electing grace. He passed by the great cities and chose a barren woman in a small hill town to bear a deliverer. The angel’s annunciation at Zorah foreshadows the greater wonders God works among the lowly and the forgotten.

Zorah also frames the whole arc of Samson’s life, from cradle to grave between two villages. His strength was never his own but the gift of the Spirit who began to move him there; his fall warns that great gifts without watchfulness end in ruin, while his last faithful prayer shows that grace can yet triumph. The God who began the work at Zorah did not abandon it at Gaza.

etymology: From the Hebrew, perhaps meaning “place of entreaty” or “asking”, from a root meaning to ask or inquire.
biblical_def: Eshtaol was a town of the lowland of Judah, always named in Scripture in company with its near neighbor Zorah, the two marking the bounds of the camp of Dan. It was first reckoned among the cities of Judah (Jos 15:33) and then among those given to the tribe of Dan (Jos 19:41). Eshtaol belongs chiefly to the history of Samson. It was “between Zorah and Eshtaol” that the Spirit of the LORD began to move him at times in the camp of Dan (Jdg 13:25), and there his body was at last laid to rest beside his father (Jdg 16:31). The town comes forward again in the migration of the Danites. When that tribe sought a place to dwell, “the children of Dan sent of their family five men from their coasts…from Zorah, and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land” (Jdg 18:2), and afterward six hundred armed men set forth from the same two towns to take Laish (Jdg 18:11). Thus Eshtaol witnessed both the stirring of the Spirit upon a single judge and the restless wandering of a whole tribe that had failed to possess its inheritance. The little town reminds us that the LORD works His purposes through ordinary places, and that the failure of a tribe to drive out its enemies bred a wandering that ended, sadly, in idolatry at Dan.
webster_summary: A lowland town of Judah, then Dan, paired with Zorah; where the Spirit moved Samson and from which the Danites went to spy out Laish.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Eshtaol is the quiet sovereignty of God in common places. Between two small villages the Spirit of the LORD began His work upon Samson; God needs no grand stage for His mighty acts. He stirs His servants where He wills.

Eshtaol also preaches a warning. The Danites went out from it not in faith to drive out the Canaanites pressing them, but in a restless search for an easier portion, a quest that ended in the idolatrous shrine at Dan. The man who will not contend in faith for the inheritance God has given often wanders into a settled disobedience. Eshtaol’s twin testimony is the moving of the Spirit and the danger of unbelief.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “house of Peor”, named for the heathen god Baal-peor worshipped there, from a root meaning to open wide.
biblical_def: Beth-peor was a place in the land of Moab, east of the Jordan, in the valley over against which Israel encamped in the last days before they crossed into Canaan. It lay in the inheritance afterward given to the tribe of Reuben (Jos 13:20). Moses recalled that “we abode in the valley over against Bethpeor” (Deu 3:29), and it was there, in the plains of Moab, that he delivered the great expositions of the law that fill Deuteronomy. The most solemn association of Beth-peor is the burial of Moses himself: “he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day” (Deu 34:6). The LORD hid the grave of His servant, that Israel might not make an idol of the place. For Beth-peor was already shadowed by idolatry, taking its very name from Baal-peor, to whom Israel joined themselves in the sin of Peor, committing whoredom with the daughters of Moab and bowing to their gods, for which a plague slew twenty and four thousand (Num 25:1–9). Thus Beth-peor holds together the giving of the law, the death of the lawgiver, and the memory of a grievous apostasy — a place where God’s word, God’s servant, and man’s idolatry meet, and where the hidden grave warns against turning even holy memory into a snare.
webster_summary: A place in Moab opposite which Israel camped, near Moses’ unknown grave, named for the idol Baal-peor.

corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is that idolatry brings plague and death, and that God hides even holy memorials lest they become idols.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Beth-peor is the deadliness of idolatry. There Israel joined itself to Baal-peor, and the anger of the LORD burned, and a plague slew thousands. The sin of Peor became a standing warning against the lust and false worship that seduce the covenant people at the very threshold of blessing.

There is a second mercy at Beth-peor. The LORD buried His servant Moses and hid the grave, that Israel might not make a shrine of it. So jealous is God for true worship that He will conceal even the resting place of His greatest prophet rather than let it become a snare. The believer learns to cling to the living God Himself, not to relics, places, or sacred memories.
roots_summary: The name means “house of Peor,” binding the place to the idol Baal-peor worshipped in that valley.
roots_lines: Beth-peor — “house of Peor,” from the idol of that name.
Beth means “house” and Peor names the Moabite god.
The god’s name may derive from a root meaning to open or gape.
It is bound to Mount Peor, where Balaam looked upon Israel (Num 23:28).
The name itself preaches the idolatry the place is remembered for.
usage: Israel encamped in the valley over against Beth-peor.
Moses was buried near Beth-peor, and no man knows the place.
The sin of Beth-peor brought a plague upon the camp of Israel.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “meadow of dancing” or “the dancing field”, from abel, a meadow, and a root for dancing.
biblical_def: Abel-meholah was a town in the Jordan valley, within the borders of the Israelite tribes east of the central highlands, remembered for two events far apart in time. The first was in the day of Gideon’s great deliverance. When the LORD set the Midianites every man’s sword against his fellow, the host fled, and the rout ran “to the border of Abelmeholah, unto Tabbath” (Jdg 7:22). Thus the town marked the edge of that famous victory, won not by Israel’s might but by the LORD’s breaking of three hundred pitchers and the cry of His sword. The second and greater association is that Abel-meholah was the home of Elisha the son of Shaphat. When the LORD commissioned the weary Elijah at Horeb, He bade him anoint Elisha to be prophet in his room. Elijah came and found him plowing — “Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was of Abelmeholah” (1Ki 19:16) — with twelve yoke of oxen, and cast his mantle upon him. Elisha rose, slew his oxen, gave the flesh to the people, and followed Elijah to be his minister (1Ki 19:19–21). The town was also named in Solomon’s provision districts (1Ki 4:12). Abel-meholah, the meadow of dancing, thus stands as the threshing-floor of a prophet’s call — the place where a plowman left the field to take up the mantle of the man of God.
webster_summary: A town in the Jordan valley, the home of the prophet Elisha and a marker on the route of Gideon’s rout of Midian.
webster_full: ABEL-MEHOLAH, a town in the Jordan valley, the birthplace of the prophet Elisha.
The fleeing Midianites were chased to its border in Gideon’s victory (Jdg 7:22).
Elijah found Elisha plowing there and cast his mantle on him (1Ki 19:16).
Elisha left his oxen and followed Elijah to be his minister (1Ki 19:21).
It was named among Solomon’s twelve provision districts (1Ki 4:12).
scriptures: And Jehu the son of Nimshi shalt thou anoint to be king over Israel: and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abelmeholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.
So he departed thence, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.

And the three hundred blew the trumpets, and the LORD set every man's sword against his fellow, even throughout all the host: and the host fled to Bethshittah in Zererath, and to the border of Abelmeholah, unto Tabbath.

corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is the sovereign call of God, who takes a plowman from his field to be a prophet, and whose victories are His own.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Abel-meholah is the sovereignty of God in calling His servants. Elisha was at his honest labor, plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, when the mantle fell upon him. He sought no office; God sought him. The call to ministry is not seized but bestowed, and the man whom God calls leaves his oxen behind.

The town’s earlier memory enforces the same truth. Gideon’s three hundred won no battle by their pitchers and trumpets; the LORD set the swords of Midian against themselves, and the rout ran past Abel-meholah. Whether in routing armies or in raising prophets, the meadow of dancing testifies that the work is God’s, and the glory His alone.
roots_summary: The name joins abel, a meadow, with a word for dancing, hence “meadow of dancing.”
roots_lines: Abel-meholah — “meadow of dancing” or “the dancing field.”
Abel means a grassy meadow, common in valley place-names.
The latter element comes from a root for dance or whirling.
It lay in the fertile Jordan valley fit for plowing and pasture.
Its sense suits the broad, green plain where Elisha drove his oxen.
usage: Elisha of Abel-meholah was plowing when Elijah found him.
The Midianites fled to the border of Abel-meholah and Tabbath.
Abel-meholah lay in the fruitful plain of the Jordan valley.

etymology: From the Hebrew, meaning “house of vanity” or “house of iniquity”, from beth, house, and aven, vanity or trouble.
biblical_def: Beth-aven, “house of vanity,” was a place in the hill country of Benjamin, lying near Ai and to the east of Bethel. In the early conquest narratives it is named as a landmark fixing the position of Ai, which was “beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel” (Jos 7:2). It marked a boundary of Benjamin’s lot (Jos 18:12), and the wilderness of Beth-aven is mentioned in Joshua’s campaign. In the days of Saul, when Jonathan smote the Philistine garrison, the battle “passed over unto Bethaven” as the men of Israel pursued (1Sa 14:23). But the name gains its sharpest edge in the prophets. After Jeroboam set up his golden calf at Bethel — whose name means “house of God” — the place became a shrine of idolatry, and the prophet Hosea, in holy scorn, renamed it Beth-aven, the house of vanity. “Though thou, Israel, play the harlot, yet let not Judah offend; and come not ye unto Gilgal, neither go ye up to Bethaven” (Hos 4:15). Again he cries that the calf-worshippers “shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven” (Hos 10:5). Thus a house once called the house of God was unmasked as a house of vanity, for what man dedicates to false worship God will name by its true character. Beth-aven stands as a rebuke to all worship that wears the name of God while serving idols.
webster_summary: A place near Ai and Bethel; Hosea’s scornful renaming of Bethel after it became a shrine of calf-worship.
webster_full: BETH-AVEN, “house of vanity,” a place in Benjamin near Ai, east of Bethel.
It fixed the location of Ai in the conquest narrative (Jos 7:2).
It marked a border of the tribe of Benjamin (Jos 18:12).
The battle of Jonathan against the Philistines passed over to it (1Sa 14:23).
Hosea used the name to mock idolatrous Bethel (Hos 4:15; Hos 10:5).
scriptures: And Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is beside Bethaven, on the east side of Bethel, and spake unto them, saying, Go up and view the country. And the men went up and viewed Ai.
So the LORD saved Israel that day: and the battle passed over unto Bethaven.
Though thou, Israel, play the harlot, yet let not Judah offend; and come not ye unto Gilgal, neither go ye up to Bethaven, nor swear, The LORD liveth.

The inhabitants of Samaria shall fear because of the calves of Bethaven: for the people thereof shall mourn over it, and the priests thereof that rejoiced on it, for the glory thereof, because it is departed from it.
corruption_summary: The lesson to recover is that God names worship by its true character: a house dedicated to idols, though styled the house of God, is a house of vanity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Beth-aven is the searching honesty of God toward false worship. Jeroboam called his shrine Bethel, the house of God, but the calf he set there made it Beth-aven, the house of vanity. The name a place wears before men cannot disguise its true character before the LORD.

This is a standing rebuke to will-worship and idolatry under a Christian label. Hosea’s scorn teaches that no sacred name sanctifies a corrupt altar. The regulative principle of worship flows from the same truth: God will be worshipped as He has commanded, not as men invent. Every house that bears His name while serving idols is, in His eyes, a Beth-aven, and He will deal with it as such.
roots_summary: The name means “house of vanity” or “iniquity,” a deliberate inversion of Bethel, “house of God.”
roots_lines: Beth-aven — “house of vanity” or “house of iniquity.”
Beth means “house” and aven means vanity, trouble, or nothingness.
It stands in pointed contrast to Beth-el, “house of God.”
Hosea coined the mocking name for idolatrous Bethel.
The same word aven often labels the emptiness of idols.
usage: Ai lay beside Beth-aven, on the east of Bethel.
Hosea called idolatrous Bethel by the name Beth-aven, house of vanity.
The men of Samaria mourned over the calves of Beth-aven.
